pos.personaBrief: Wikipedia says transition speed matters more than possession, and Trapattoni dismissed sterile possession; the team won through quick transitions against opponents' rearguard.

pro.personaBrief: Quick transitions to put the rearguard in difficulty (Wikipedia), a pragmatic style with remnants of catenaccio; safe, vertical play over risky build-up.

est.personaBrief: Zona mista keeps the intended organisational structure with each player having a defined function and covering for those who leave their zone (Spielverlagerung, Wikipedia), while striker and attackers are not rondo-style combinators.

lar.personaBrief: Juve's stars (Platini, Tardelli, Brady, Rossi, Bettega) were central; width came from the advancing left back Cabrini as an added winger rather than classic wingers.

blo.personaBrief: Remnants of catenaccio, results-first and counter-attacking; no evidence of pressing, so it defends in compact lines and waits, not high pressing.

mar.personaBrief: Defining feature is man-marking on the playmaker or fantasista (Gentile) mixed with zonal cover; Trapattoni called man-marking a religion yet adopted zona mista.

pla.personaBrief: Pragmatism as a philosophy of life; the coach adapted to the players available ('wine with the grapes you have') and set up marking to neutralise the opposing star.

res.personaBrief: Results first, pragmatism, calcio all'italiana as a trademark; six scudetti and European trophies; solid defensive game management.

sis.personaBrief: Everyone has a function in the system (each player performs a different function), players are free to do what the coach says; stars like Platini fit into the structure and the collective prevails.

jog.personaBrief: Gritty defenders like Gentile who knew how to foul and intimidate, physical duels, but also a technical trequartista like Brady and Platini.

bas.personaBrief: Juve invested in young Italian players but won titles with seasoned veterans like Zoff, Gentile, Scirea and signed stars; experience first.

lid.personaBrief: Padre padrone style: the coach sends back a player to his father, orders are followed; discipline and authority over negotiation.
